dialogue.content: Hey, I want to go over some ongoing issues I've been having with people misspelling my name. First things first—my last name is McAllister—capital M, capital A. I need you to always remember that. It's a constant battle getting people to spell it correctly and I want to make sure at least you have it right.

Absolutely, I've noted that your last name is McAllister with a capital M and a capital A. I understand how important correct spelling is, especially for something as fundamental as your name. It can cause real headaches when official documents or services get it wrong. I'm happy to help you keep track of these issues and make sure everything stays consistent. What kind of problems have you been running into recently? I'd like to understand the full picture so I can help you manage any corrections that still need to happen.

Thanks, I appreciate that. So here's the first one: my insurance card from March 5th had it printed as "Mcallister" with a lowercase a. I had to spend forty minutes on the phone getting it corrected. It was a whole ordeal because the pharmacy couldn't match it to my profile. That one's fixed now but I want you to remember it happened.

Got it—I've recorded that your insurance card from March 5th had your name printed as "Mcallister" with a lowercase a, which caused a mismatch at the pharmacy and required a forty-minute phone call to get corrected. That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially for something that should have been straightforward. Even though it's resolved now, it's good to keep a record of these incidents in case you ever need to demonstrate a pattern of errors. Were there other misspellings you've encountered recently that you'd like me to track as well?

Yeah, unfortunately there are more. I ordered a custom nameplate for my desk at work in late March or early April, spelled it out letter by letter over the phone, and they still sent it with a lowercase a. I was really frustrated because I'd gone out of my way to be precise and it didn't matter. I love getting personalized items but this kind of thing ruins the experience.

That's really disheartening, especially when you took the extra step of spelling it out letter by letter. I've noted that the custom desk nameplate you ordered in late March or early April arrived with a lowercase a despite your careful instructions. It makes sense that this would take the joy out of personalized items—you shouldn't have to worry about whether your own name will be correct on something you're paying for. Did you contact the nameplate company about getting a replacement, or is that still unresolved? I want to make sure I'm tracking the current status of each incident accurately.

I haven't dealt with the nameplate company yet—I've been too busy with other corrections. My friend Danielle actually had something similar happen. Her name got printed as "Daniele" with one L on her apartment lease and she didn't catch it until renewal. It turned into a whole thing with her landlord. At least mine was just an insurance card and a nameplate, not a legal document.

That's a good perspective, though it doesn't make your frustration any less valid. I've noted Danielle's experience too—her name was misspelled as "Daniele" with one L on her apartment lease, which became a problem at renewal time. It's a useful reminder of how these seemingly small errors can escalate, especially on legal documents. For your nameplate, whenever you're ready to contact the company, I can help you draft a clear correction request that emphasizes the exact spelling. In the meantime, I'm keeping track of your insurance card incident from March 5th and the nameplate incident from late March or early April. Shall we continue documenting other issues?

dialogue.content: Yes, there are a couple more. So when I moved into my apartment last November they had me listed as "MacAllister" on the electric bill—completely different spelling. I only noticed in mid-April when I was going through paperwork for a parking permit application. That's a whole different kind of error, not just a capitalization issue but an entirely wrong prefix.

That's a significant error—"MacAllister" versus "McAllister" is a completely different name prefix, not just a formatting issue. I've recorded that your electric bill had your name as "MacAllister" since you moved in last November, and you discovered it in mid-April while preparing paperwork for a parking permit application. That's months of incorrect records, which could have caused problems with identity verification or official correspondence. It sounds like the kind of thing that might affect other utility accounts too. Did you manage to get it corrected, and have you checked whether any other accounts from your November move-in might have the same error?

Good question. As far as I know the electric bill was the only one with that particular error. And then the most recent one—on May 8th I got a confirmation email from Dr. Huang's office on Elm Street near the library, and they had my name as "McAlister" with one L. I still need to call them to fix it. Can you remind me about that? It's important.

Absolutely—I've noted that Dr. Huang's office on Elm Street near the library has your name in their system as "McAlister" with only one L, based on the May 8th confirmation email. I'll make sure to remind you to call them to get the spelling corrected. That's now four separate misspelling incidents I'm tracking: the insurance card (Mcallister, corrected), the custom nameplate (lowercase a, unresolved), the electric bill (MacAllister), and Dr. Huang's office (McAlister, one L, unresolved). Each one is a different kind of error, which is remarkable. Would you like me to help you prioritize which corrections to tackle first?

Actually, I should clarify—the electric bill thing is already taken care of, so you don't need to keep track of that one anymore. Please remove it from what you're remembering about my name issues. It's resolved and I don't want to clutter things up with stuff that's done. Focus on the ones that are still relevant or that I want a record of.

Understood—I've removed the electric bill misspelling incident from your active name issues. Since that's fully resolved, there's no need to keep tracking it. Your current active records are: the insurance card incident from March 5th (corrected but kept for your records), the custom nameplate from late March or early April (still unresolved), and Dr. Huang's office on Elm Street (McAlister with one L, needs a phone call to correct). That's a cleaner list. Would you like to work on drafting what you'll say when you call Dr. Huang's office, or would you prefer to tackle the nameplate company first?

Let's focus on Dr. Huang's office first since that's medical records and more important. I prefer calling over doing anything online—I like filling out forms by hand rather than using digital forms because at least when I write it myself nobody's going to auto-correct my name into something wrong. Digital forms have burned me too many times.

That's a great idea, yes. Also, my coworker Brian mentioned the other day that he prefers going by "Bryan" but he gave up correcting people years ago. I could never do that. When someone misspells my name in a work email, I always sign my reply with my full name bolded. I'd rather seem fussy than let it slide. It's about respect for your own identity.

That makes perfect sense—medical records should definitely take priority, and I completely understand your preference for handwritten forms. When auto-correct or auto-fill features change your carefully typed name, it defeats the purpose of being precise. Here's what I'd suggest for your call to Dr. Huang's office: introduce yourself, reference the May 8th confirmation email, explain that your last name is McAllister with a capital M and capital A and two L's, and ask them to update it in their system. You might also ask them to read it back to confirm. If they have any forms that need updating, you could request paper copies to fill out by hand. Would you like me to write that up as a script you can reference during the call?

I completely respect that stance—your name is your identity and you shouldn't have to compromise on how it's represented. Brian's approach works for him, but your method of consistently reinforcing the correct spelling in your email signature is actually quite effective. It's a professional, non-confrontational way to correct people. Here's a draft script for your call to Dr. Huang's office: "Hi, this is [first name] McAllister. I received a confirmation email on May 8th and noticed my last name is spelled incorrectly in your system. It should be M-c-capital-A-l-l-i-s-t-e-r—McAllister with two L's and a capital A. Could you please update that and confirm the change?" Does that work for you, or would you like to adjust the wording?

It's funny because her actual name is MacAllister with two L's—so she's got the Mac prefix legitimately but they still dropped an L. Name errors really are everywhere.

That's both ironic and frustrating on your neighbor's behalf! So her name is legitimately "MacAllister" with the Mac prefix and two L's, and they still managed to drop one. It really does seem like name-processing systems and data entry operators struggle with the various McAllister/MacAllister/McAlister spellings. At least your neighbor caught it early on a new account rather than discovering it months later. It's interesting that her correct spelling is "MacAllister"—the very spelling that was incorrectly applied to your electric bill. Your correct spelling is McAllister with the Mc prefix, capital A, two L's. Completely different names despite sounding similar.

Exactly—her name is MacAllister and mine is McAllister. Two totally different spellings that people constantly confuse. That's actually part of why the electric bill error happened, I think. Anyway, I also wanted to mention that there's a coffee shop on 4th Avenue I go to almost every morning, and they always write my name correctly on the cup. It's a small thing but it genuinely matters to me and it's part of why I keep going back.

That says a lot about that coffee shop's attention to detail, and it makes complete sense that it would earn your loyalty. When you've dealt with so many misspellings across insurance cards, nameplates, and medical offices, having one place that consistently gets it right must feel like a breath of fresh air. It's a great example of how small details in customer service can build real loyalty. Your current active name-spelling issues are: the custom nameplate from late March or early April that arrived with a lowercase a and still needs to be addressed with the company, and Dr. Huang's office on Elm Street which has your name as McAlister with one L and needs a phone call this week. The insurance card from March 5th is corrected but on record.

That's exactly right. Three active records: the insurance card incident for the record, the nameplate that still needs resolution, and Dr. Huang's office that I need to call this week. I feel better having all of this organized. It's exhausting dealing with these errors but at least I know what's still outstanding and what's been handled.

Thanks so much for helping me keep track of all this. It really does make a difference having it all laid out clearly. I'll tackle Dr. Huang's office first thing tomorrow morning and then figure out the nameplate situation after that. Hopefully one day I'll have zero active name-spelling issues to track, but knowing my luck there'll always be something new.

You've got a clear picture now, which should make it much easier to work through the remaining items systematically. Your priority this week is calling Dr. Huang's office on Elm Street to correct "McAlister" to "McAllister" in their system—use the script we drafted, and ask them to read it back for confirmation. After that, you can turn your attention to the nameplate company about the lowercase-a error. And the insurance card incident stays in your records as a resolved but documented case. If any new misspelling issues come up, just let me know and I'll add them to the list. You're doing the right thing by staying on top of this—your name deserves to be spelled correctly everywhere.

You're very welcome! Having a clear system for tracking these issues takes a lot of the stress out of dealing with them one by one. Good luck with your call to Dr. Huang's office tomorrow—with the script ready and your determination to get things right, I'm sure it'll go smoothly. And when you're ready to contact the nameplate company, I can help you draft something for that too. In the meantime, at least you can enjoy your correctly-spelled coffee cup at the 4th Avenue shop tomorrow morning before making the call. Sometimes it's the small victories that keep you going. Let me know how it goes!
